summary: Alf Sommerfelt was a linguist who founded the Norwegian Association for Linguistics in 1924. He served as professor of linguistics at the University of Oslo from 1931 to 1962.

Alf Torp worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned an M.A. at the University of Oslo under Sophus Bugge and a Ph.D. at Leipzig under Ernst Windisch and Georg Curtius, later serving as professor at Oslo (1894–1914).

Alfons Fürst is a scholar of religious studies and history/archaeology. He studied at the University of Regensburg and under Richard von Garbe at Tübingen. In 2000, he became professor at the University of Münster.

Alfons Hilka was a scholar of linguistics and Indology. He studied at Breslau, Berlin, and Poitiers under Alfred Hillebrandt, Adolf Tobler, and Carl Appel. He held professorships at Greifswald (1918) and Göttingen (1921).

Alfons Klaus Weidert worked in linguistics and Tibetology. He completed his Ph.D. at Heidelberg University around 1968–1971, held a DFG research position from circa 1979 to 1984, and became PD at Kiel University in 1982.

Alfons Nehring was a linguist and Indologist. He studied at Berlin and under Otto Schrader at Breslau (Ph.D. c. 1915). He held posts at Breslau, Marquette, Fordham, and Würzburg, where he was professor of Indogermanistik (1952–1958).

Alfons Väth was a scholar in history, archaeology, and Indology. He taught English and Indian history at St. Xavier's College, Mumbai, from around 1911 to 1914 and edited Die Katholischen Missionen from 1918 to 1925.

Alfonsa Ferrari worked in Tibetology, Indology, and Buddhist studies. She studied under Carlo Formichi, Giuseppe Tucci, Louis Renou, Jacques Bacot, and Marcelle Lalou at Rome and Paris, becoming professor of Sanskrit at Sapienza University of Rome in 1951.

Alfred Bloch was an Indologist and linguist who completed his Ph.D. at the University of Basel in 1939. He spent his career at Basel, serving as Privatdozent from 1942 and lecturer in Indogermanistik and Hebrew from 1949 to 1982.

Alfred Bloom was a scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and Japanology. He earned his Ph.D. at Harvard under Masatoshi Nagatomi, taught at the University of Oregon (1961–1970) and Hawaii (1970–1986), and was dean of IBS (1986–1994).

Alfred Chilton Pearson was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He was educated at King's College School, Highgate School, and Christ's College, Cambridge, where he studied under John Peile around 1879–1883.

Alfred Cooper Woolner was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Trinity College, Oxford, under Arthur Anthony Macdonell. He served as Principal of Oriental College (1903) and Dean of University Instruction at the University of the Punjab (1903–1936).
Alfred Cort Haddon studied at Christ's College, Cambridge. He held academic posts at the University of Cambridge (1879–1880, 1900–1926) and the Royal College of Science for Ireland (1880–1901).
Alfred Darby was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied at St Augustine's College, Canterbury, and earned a B.D. at Durham University by 1908, later holding a post at Rajaram College.
Alfred Edward Housman was a scholar in linguistics and other fields. He was educated at St John's College, Oxford, and held a post at University College London from around 1892 to 1911.

Alfred Ernout was a linguist who studied at Lille, the EPHE, and the Sorbonne under Antoine Meillet. He held professorships at the University of Lille, the University of Paris, the EPHE, and the Collège de France (1944–1951).

Alfred Forke was a scholar of Sinology and philosophy. He studied under Carl Arendt and at Geneva, Berlin, and Rostock. He held posts at the Seminar for Oriental Languages, UC Berkeley, and the University of Hamburg (1923–1935).

Alfred Foucher specialized in Indology, archaeology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at the ENS and under Sylvain Lévi at the EPHE. He served as professor at the University of Paris and directed the DAFA (1922–1925).

Alfred Gell studied under Edmund Leach at Trinity College, Cambridge, and earned his Ph.D. at the LSE. He held lectureships at Sussex (1972–1974), the Australian National University (1974–1979), and the London School of Economics (1979–1997).

Alfred Hillebrandt was an Indologist and linguist who studied under Adolf Friedrich Stenzler at Breslau and Martin Haug at Munich. He spent his career at the University of Breslau, serving as professor from 1887 to 1921.
